stories.title: Minister's claims over solicitors' dispute action 'false'
stories.summary: A solicitor working in criminal legal aid has described the comments by the Minister for Justice that solicitors had deliberately targeted rape cases in their dispute as beneath the dignity of his office. Eoghan O'Sullivan, who works for Powderly Solicitors in Dublin, said criminal defence solicitors from Dublin and right around the country withdrew all of their services from all courts yesterday. This included cases of rape listed in the Central Criminal Court as well as cases in the Circuit Criminal Court and the District Court. The Central Criminal Court deals only with serious crimes such as murder and rape. There were no murder cases on yesterday’s list. A number of other cases involving other alleged offences were also adjourned in the lower courts. A majority of solicitors working in criminal legal aid across the country have been in dispute with Minister Jim O'Callaghan since a new €520 flat-fee payment for legal aid cases was introduced in July. The minister insists that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts; solicitors continue to provide representation, and defendants continue to receive legal services throughout the State.

stories.summary: The Minister for Justice will today call on solicitors to explain why cases involving allegations of rape were in his words, "deliberately affected" today in the dispute over changes to the legal aid scheme. Minister Jim O'Callaghan will tell the Oireachtas Justice Committee that the public are entitled to an answer as to why this was the case. A majority of solicitors working in criminal legal aid across the country have been in dispute with Minister O’Callaghan since a new €520 flat-fee payment for legal aid cases was introduced in July. The Minister insists that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts; solicitors continue to provide representation, and defendants continue to receive legal services throughout the State. However, he will acknowledge that, particularly in Dublin, a number of solicitors have withdrawn services which has impacted court hearings. But Minister O’Callaghan will state that despite this, in the Central Criminal Court yesterday, the majority of cases proceeded without issue.

stories.title: Minister questions university funding gap figure
stories.summary: Minister for Higher and Further Education James Lawless has said the demand from Irish universities for €250 million to bridge a core funding gap is "significantly in excess" of the previously agreed figure. In 2022, the gap in core funding for Irish universities was identified as €307 million. The Government agreed to close that gap over successive budgets at a rate of €25 million per year. Five budgets later, the gap is €130 million, according to the Irish University Association it increases to €250 million if pay and pensions are included. In Budget 2027, €10 million was awarded to Funding the Future, which will plug some of the universities' funding gap. Minister Lawless said, in addition to that: "I gave almost €200 million in things like pay awards in terms of pension deficits being addressed."

stories.title: Why are Irish households not using dynamic electricity tariffs?
stories.summary: Analysis: Electricity suppliers have had to provide these tariffs since June, but most people have not noticed that they're on offer and can save them money By Dan Dransfield, Niamh Power and Evan Finegan, Munster Technological University Irish households now pay the highest electricity prices in Europe, so choosing the right tariff matters. Since June, the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) has required the five largest electricity suppliers to offer a dynamic tariff, but most people won't have noticed. On a standard tariff, unit prices are set in advance by the supplier. On a dynamic tariff, part of the price changes every half hour in line with the wholesale market. When the wind is strong and demand is low, wholesale electricity is cheap. On the other hand, it can be very expensive on a calm winter evening. The aim of dynamic tariffs is to encourage households to use more power when it is plentiful and cleaner, and less when the grid is under pressure. Several countries, including Spain, Norway and the UK, already have versions of these tariffs. Our research looked at whether Irish homes are in a position to benefit, and whether the tariffs on offer are designed to deliver what they promise. We used at least a year of half-hourly smart meter data from 41 Irish homes with solar panels. Two thirds also had an electric car, almost 60% had a home battery and about a third had a heat pump. These homes can move large loads such as car charging to cheaper times. We calculated what each home would have paid on 22 tariffs from the five largest suppliers, using their actual consumption and did not assume any change in behaviour.

stories.title: Curfews in France after weekend violence
stories.summary: Curfews were in force in parts of northern France overnight after the country was rocked by some of its worst street violence in years. The French government imposed curfews in four northern cities tonight and tomorrow night, while separate restrictions were also being introduced in parts of central Paris. France may also impose new curfews in areas where needed today, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said. "Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight," Mr Lecornu wrote on X. "Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors." Curfews came into effect at 8pm local time last night (7pm Irish time) and ran to 5am (4am Irish time) in Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain. The same curfew will apply tonight. Authorities also enforced a curfew covering Place de la République and the streets around Les Halles in central Paris, which was in place until 5am local time (4am Irish time).

The visitors arrived in Galway with a squad littered with British and Irish Lions and international players. They might be ageing internationals, but their players include the most recent Lions captain in Maro Itoje, alongside Jamie George, Ben Earl, Owen Farrell, Tomos Williams and Elliot Daly. stories.title: Two-time All-Star Rushe calls time on Dublin career
stories.summary: Two-time Dublin All-Star Liam Rushe has confirmed his retirement from inter-county hurling. The 36-year-old Na Fianna man made a surprise return to the panel last season ahead of the championship, ending a four-year exodus having last played in the 2022 Leinster SHC. He came back into the starting side for Niall Ó Ceallacháin - starting at centre half-back in the Leinster final loss to Galway. Rushe's season came to an end last weekend as Na Fianna lost to Cuala in the Dublin semi-final and on Sunday, he was on punditry duty with TG4 for the Offaly SHC final between Kilcormac-Killoughey and Ballinamere. Follwing Kilcormac-Killoughgey's 0-19 to 0-17 win, Rushe confirmed he wouldn't be returning to the Dublin squad. "Sin mo rás rite ag an leibhéal idir chontae (that's my race run at county)," said the 2011 Young Hurler of the Year.

stories.title: O'Donoghue proud as Munster victorious on emotional night
stories.summary: It's never easy for Munster, and they are often an emotional team, but this week was like no other. Saturday night’s 33-25 win over Racing 92 came ten years and one day on from the sad passing of then-Munster head coach Anthony Foley, on the eve of a fixture against the same team. Few moments summed up like the poignancy of the occasion like what followed the full-time whistle, as a large group of players, coaches and staff gathered in the middle of the Cork field to sing the club’s unique anthem, "Stand Up and Fight". Double-centurion Jack O’Donoghue was a young 22-year-old when Munster did the same thing in their win over Glasgow Warriors, in Thomond Park on the day after Foley’s funeral. He is a wise 32-year-old veteran now, but the emotion remains the same for the Waterford man. "For me personally, it was very emotional", the Waterford native said. "I stood in that circle ten years ago as a young fella just coming through. "I was asked after the game what Axel meant to me and he gave me my first opportunity. He put time and effort into me and sitting down as an academy player, watching videos, watching training and teaching me the little intricate bits of the game.

stories.title: Mariah Carey wins dismissal of brother's lawsuit
stories.summary: Mariah Carey has won the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit brought by her brother over claims made in her bestselling memoir, The Meaning of Mariah Carey. A New York judge ruled on Monday that Morgan Carey had failed to sufficiently establish "actual malice" in his case against the singer. Morgan sued his sister in 2021, alleging that her 2020 book had damaged his reputation by suggesting he had sold cocaine and spent time in prison. His original lawsuit also challenged passages portraying him as violent. Most of his claims were dismissed in 2022, but two passages relating to alleged drug dealing and imprisonment were allowed to proceed. In the latest ruling, Judge Leslie A Stroth said: "The Court finds that Plaintiff has not sufficiently pleaded actual malice on the part of Defendant."

stories.title: Are you cheating on your partner with your phone?
stories.summary: Are you suffering from 'attention infidelity'? American author Daniel Cox coined the term to explain how screen habits intrude on face-to-face connection and emotional presence. Helen Vaughan, Director at Maynooth Counselling and Psychotherapy, explains. Listen back above. To paraphrase Princess Diana: there are now three players in most relationships. And one of them isn't even a person. Phones have infiltrated the majority of our relationships, whether it's a mindless scroll in bed, liking posts throughout that film you promised you'd watch together, or missing out on sharing special moments in favour of consuming yet more online content. We now have a term for this thoroughly modern relationship hurdle: 'attention infidelity'. But what's behind its rise, and what can we do to curb it? Accredited psychotherapist Vaughan says it boils down to "lack of connection" and the fact that we all have a device that is engineered to pull our focus, which doesn't help. "It’s designed to be addictive, it is, and if you don’t consciously uncouple with your phone, it can take over, and it can interrupt those small opportunities couples have to connect with each other in the morning, in the evening and at the weekend, whenever it is that you have a bit of downtime", she says.

stories.title: Two men appear in court over car theft and M50 pursuit
stories.summary: Two men charged in connection with a traffic pursuit in which a stolen car allegedly drove on the wrong side of the M50 in Dublin yesterday evening have been denied bail. Daniel Brown, 22, of Hampton Wood in Dublin 11 was charged with four counts of dangerous driving, being in a stolen Volkswagen Golf Estate and possession of cannabis. Co-defendant Adam White, 25, also from Hampton Wood, was charged with being in the stolen car and possession of cannabis for sale or supply. The pair are also accused of having a stolen key to a Toyota car and theft implements. Garda Dylan Toner from Coolock Garda Station gave evidence of the arrest, charge, and caution, and objected to bail for the pair, who had no solicitors to represent them because of the escalating industrial dispute over legal aid fee reforms introduced in July. They opted to represent themselves and had separate hearings in which Garda Dylan Toner told Judge Karen Dowling they made no reply when charged.

stories.title: Four candidates to contest Seanad bye-election seat
stories.summary: Four candidates are to contest the forthcoming Seanad bye-election for the remaining vacancy in the Oireachtas. The vote to fill a seat on the Seanad's Cultural and Educational panel was triggered by the success of Fine Gael's Sean Kyne in the Galway West Dáil bye-election in May. The Seanad returning officer ruled on nominations yesterday with ballot papers to be issued to those voting on Friday 23 October. The poll closes on Friday 6 November. There are 233 members of the Dáil and Seanad who are eligible to vote, of which 51.5% are representatives of Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael. Former Dublin city lord mayor Ray McAdam has been selected as the Fine Gael candidate, having ran unsuccessfully in the Dublin Central bye-election in May to fill the seat of his party colleague Pascal Donohoe, receiving 10.67% of the vote. Success for the Dublin City Councillor would be regarded as strategically important for Fine Gael, with the party currently without Oireachtas representation in Mr McAdam's Dáil constituency of Dublin Central and the neighbouring constituency of Dublin North West.

stories.title: Zelensky says no early warning of latest Russian strikes
stories.summary: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed. Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructureacross Ukraine. Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones in attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odesa in the south and Volyn and Rivne in the west. The strikes killed two people in Kyiv and the nearby region and two more people in the industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said. Tensions are running high between President Zelensky and President Donald Trump's administration over US support for Ukraine and Washington's approach to Russia. "Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Mr Zelensky said on the Telegram app.

stories.title: Cawley: Marvellous Moylan a perfect fit for Brentford
stories.summary: Moylan was on the goal trail again on Saturday, scoring the first and making the second for Cardiff in a 2-2 draw at Middlesbrough. That brings the former Shelbourne schemer to a total of six goals and three assists in just 11 Championship games so far this season. That's been enough to convince Cawley that Moylan's form - and class - are not just temporary. "It's only early days, you don't want to be getting too carried away but Cardiff will be doing well to hold onto him if he keeps up this level of form, he's absolutely flying." Moylan earned promotion from League 1 with Lincoln City last term having moved across the channel after excelling at Shels. Cardiff, runners up to Moylan's Imps, also made the leap to the second tier - with Moylan in turn making the move to Wales. Many observers on this side of the water feel his next move, should he make one, could see him add to the ever-growing Irish contingent at Keith Andrews' Brentford - particularly with his old Shels boss, Damien Duff, now part of Andrews' back-room team as assistant manager. "He could go up another level and I think he will," Cawley predicted.

stories.title: Dublin SFC: O'Callaghan & McMorrow excel in Cuala stroll
stories.summary: Con O'Callaghan netted twice as Cuala returned to the summit of the Dublin SFC, easing to their second title success in three seasons with a rout of outclassed Castleknock. Laying the platform for victory with an unanswered 1-09 in the first half, the 2025 All-Ireland winners surged to another landmark win, the club's second ever title. King Con finished with 2-05 for the Dalkey outfit who trailed briefly early on before hitting the afterburners and burning off a Castleknock side that simply had no response to the onslaught. Jamie Conroy grabbed the other goal for Cuala but that came in the closing minutes of the second half and, in truth, the game as a contest was over at that stage. Dublin duo Eoin Kennedy and Charlie McMorrow contributed two points apiece while even veteran Sky Blues icon Michael Fitzsimons, wearing his usual number three, added a brace of points on a famous day for the club. With the Cuala hurlers also preparing for a senior county final, a dream double of titles remains on the cards.

stories.title: Brentford contact police after 'dangerous' incident
stories.summary: Brentford have contacted police following a "dangerous" and "potentially very harmful" incident which involved an "item being kicked from a height towards the field of play" in their 2-1 defeat against Liverpool. The club have commented after footage of an individual appearing to hit a rugby ball towards the Gtech Community Stadium pitch from a nearby rooftop during Saturday's match circulated on social media. A statement from the Bees read: "Brentford are aware of an incident involving an item being kicked from a height towards the field of play during Saturday's match against Liverpool. "The matter has been referred to the police and the club are supporting the relevant authorities in their investigation to help identify those responsible and take appropriate action, which may result in criminal prosecution. "The matchday safety of fans, staff, players and officials is of utmost importance, and the club will support all efforts to ensure action is taken." Alexander Isak struck a late winner as Liverpool came from behind to beat nine-man Brentford.

stories.title: Lancaster thrilled by Connacht's European response
stories.summary: Connacht boss Stuart Lancaster believes that his side's thrilling 45-36 Champions Cup victory over Saracens was the perfect response to a heavy defeat to Glasgow in last week’s United Rugby Championship clash. Cian Prendergast and Ciaran Frawley scored two tries apiece as Connacht turned on the style in Galway, with Cathal Forde, Shamus Hurley-Langton and Caolin Blade also crossing the line. The result and performance was in marked contrast to last week’s 36-19 URC defeat to Glasgow in Scotstoun. "Yeah, I was buzzing, really. It was an amazing atmosphere, wasn’t it?" he said. "You know, I think I was obviously disappointed at how we lost last week against Glasgow, but it was down to four maul tries, and I knew if we could address that, and we had enough in our armoury to challenge any team, really. "We proved it last season, and I could see in training we had a real edge this week, and perhaps the disappointment of Glasgow was inside us.

stories.title: This Modern Love: Emma Gilleece's ode to Irish architecture
stories.summary: 'First of all we must cleanse our minds of imitation, and, in disengaging ourselves of antique manners, bring our work to simplicity and truth shaping each building to necessity, and look for beauty in chastity and proportions. That is the task before all Irish art, and it is especially the task before Irish architecture'. This was the clarion call Darrell Figgis (1882-1925), the co-drafter of the Irish Free State’s constitution, made on 22 March 1922 in his address to the Architectural Association of Ireland. As a member of the Gaelic League, he understood cultural self-expression to extend beyond language and into the built environment. In his view, the continued reliance on the historicist architectural traditions of Britain, Ireland’s former coloniser, risked constraining the development of a distinct national identity and inhibiting the evolution of an indigenous architectural language. This presented an opportunity to project the nation’s forward-looking ambitions through a contemporary architectural language, free from the ornamentation and stylistic conventions associated with imperial rule, from early Georgian to Edwardian. Modernism was particularly well suited to a nation seeking to define itself as an independent republic, reflecting aspirations towards greater social equality, civic progress and economic self-sufficiency and even lent itself to the conservatism of the Catholic Church. This book celebrates the architects, craftspeople, artists, clients, and policymakers who embraced this vision, as well as the subsequent generations who carried forward the principles of modernism through the Free State and into the Republic. The first milestone in Irish modernity was the construction of the hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, overseen by the Cumann na nGaedheal administration of the 1920s. Political and cultural transformations followed with the arrival of a Fianna Fáil government in 1932, which advanced protectionism and began an economic war (1933-7) with Britain. Among other things, this hugely affected the availability of building materials. Nevertheless, in that same year, the Housing (Financial and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act came into force to provide local authorities with state funding for the provision of houses for working class families who had been cleared from the slums of Dublin, Cork, Limerick, and Waterford. Between 1932 and 1942, despite Ireland’s economic vulnerability, 12,000 houses per year were built. Our modern hospitals also evolved at this time with the establishment of the Hospitals Trust Board to administer the funds raised by the Hospital Sweepstakes Fund. The modernist principles of hygiene, free circulation, light, and lack of ornament were perfectly suited to such buildings and the resulting hospitals came to embody the spirit of medical and architectural progress. During the ‘Emergency’, despite our neutral status, hundreds of defensive structures were rapidly built around our coast and were modernist in material and form. After the War, it was, strangely enough, the Catholic Church, the stewards of conservatism, oppression, and censorship, who would be the country’s greatest patron of modernist architecture and art in the churches built after the Second Vatican Council of 1962 to 1965. Modernist architecture seemed to symbolise a Church that was more liberal and open, more orientated to the future, and more in keeping with the outward-looking economics and ‘invitation to industrialisation’ pursued by Lemass’ government, leading to the membership of the EEC in January 1973. The scope of this research runs from 1927 to the late 1970s. This survey of fifty structures is certainly not an exhaustive list. Instead, its ambition is to draw attention to structures that are often unloved or just overlooked and to show that these can be found across the country, contradicting the common belief that architectural innovation and novelty can only be found in our capital or at least only in our major cities. Every county in the Republic of Ireland is covered by at least one structure, ranging from government buildings, schools, post offices to a handball alley, garda station, and a water tower. Some buildings are iconic (and therefore already familiar to the reader), others are little-known gems, but what they all have in common is that they are irreplaceable. Conscious that architecture is, of course, something that is best experienced in person, this book is designed to fit into your bag or the glove compartment of your car to bring on trips around the country. Such an introduction is a springboard to entice the reader to seek out these structures and, perhaps, take a deeper-dive into the history of this quite everyday built heritage. The lamentable near absence of women architects in this volume - represented by only one building out of fifty - mirrors the broader scarcity of women in Irish architecture and engineering throughout the early to mid-twentieth century. Societal expectations, restrictive marriage bars, and exclusionary professional cultures made it exceptionally difficult for women to enter, remain in, or advance within these fields. Against this backdrop, the achievement of Angela Jupe, the architect of the Braun factory in Co. Carlow stands out: leading a design team at the Industrial Development Agency (IDA) in the early 1970s was a rare and significant accomplishment for a woman in the profession. Nevertheless, the book highlights instances in which women artists made significant contributions to the overall conception and experience of architectural projects, including the façade of the Department of Trade and Enterprise and the interior artistic programme of St Aengus Church. In addition, anecdotal accounts indicate that the wives of a number of male architects, who had professions for their creativity pre-marriage, were involved in advising on interior design and landscaping schemes. Such contributions, however, were seldom recorded in official project documentation and therefore remain largely absent from the historical record. May this book be the starting point for oral histories on these undocumented contributions.

This presented an [[deis|opportunity]] to project the nation’s forward-looking [[uaillmhianta|ambitions]] through a contemporary architectural [[teanga|language]], free from the [[maisiú|ornamentation]] and stylistic [[coinbhinsiúin|conventions]] associated with [[impiriúil|imperial]] rule, from [[luath|early]] Georgian to Edwardian. stories.title: 7 habits of successful savers in Ireland
stories.summary: Financial advisor Ralph Benson of Moneycube.ie shares his top tips for saving money in Ireland. Being good with money needn't create drama. It’s about establishing regular positive habits that set you on the right course over the medium term. Successful savers get stuck in. It’s all too easy to push saving some cash into next month’s payslip. There are lots of demands on our money, so make sure to pay yourself first. When income lands in your current account, before you do anything else, put some away in regular savings. And however small, first means first: before your housing, food or other costs. The most sustainable approach is to establish a small, regular habit now, and build it as you go. The alternative, deciding month-to-month how much you’ll save, requires more discipline, and you’re more likely to give up or save less. You’ll be much more motivated once you picture what you’re saving for. Most of us have short, medium, and long-term savings needs. Save for them separately.

stories.title: France to impose new curfews where necessary, says PM
stories.summary: France will impose new curfews in areas where needed, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the measures introduced in several cities the previous day had "helped keep the night calm". France was rocked on Saturday by some of its worst rioting in recent years, just six months before the country elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron. Accused of failing to anticipate and contain the street violence, the government has pledged to restore order, and had announced partial curfews in Paris and some other cities yesterday. "Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight," Mr Lecornu wrote on X. "Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors," he said. Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France.

stories.title: State 'stepping up to the plate' with Stack apology - son
stories.summary: The son of a prison officer who was shot by the IRA in 1983 and later died has said that the State is "stepping up to the plate" by issuing an apology over the investigations into his death. Brian Stack was chief prison officer at Portlaoise Prison when he was shot by the IRA in Dublin in March 1983. He died 18 months later. There were three separate garda investigations into Mr Stack's death, but no one was ever brought to justice for his killing. On Wednesday, his family will receive a State apology in the Dáil from Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Mr Stack said: "The most important person in all this is my dad, and we must not lose sight of that. He was doing a very difficult job for the State at a very difficult time in our history and he was awarded the Prison Service's highest bravery reward for doing that job. "And, it [the apology] means a great deal of comfort. It brings a great deal of comfort to my family, especially my mother, that the State are now officially recognising the failings that occurred in three separate investigations, particularly that first investigation."

stories.title: Pointed questions raised ahead of new Troubles Bill
stories.summary: Why is the biggest single atrocity of the Troubles not covered by the new Troubles Legacy Bill moving through Westminster? It was one of the more pointed questions raised in the House of Commons this week by Unionist MPs during a debate on re-introducing new legislation to deal with Northern Ireland's bloody past - in the same week that new revelations about that past were emerging in the Omagh bombing inquiry. Foremost among those revelations was a document - read into the record by veteran BBC investigative journalist John Ware - a handwritten note detailing the contents of a call received by what appears to be an Irish Army NCO at Finner Camp, Co Donegal, the night before the Omagh bombing, urging the deployment of Irish and Northern Ireland security forces to the backroads leading to Omagh. The origin of the document is unclear (it refers to "this section": DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the document came "from the South"), but it was certainly made after 27 August 1998 - that is at least 12 days after the Omagh bomb had ended 31 lives. The one page extract from the handwritten note published by the Inquiry on Thursday appears to show that a person whose name is redacted did not log the phone call, and did not report it up the chain of command to the 'SDO’ (Station Duty Officer) at Custume Barracks, Athlone. The note further states that the person whose name is redacted was interviewed by ‘local GS’ (Garda Siochana) on either Sunday 16 August or Monday 17 August about the call.

stories.title: UK jobs market shows some signs of recovery
stories.summary: British workers have seen another small rise in the pace of pay growth and there were other signs of a small recovery in the jobs market, according to data which could bolster the case for a Bank of England interest rate hike next month. Average weekly earnings, excluding bonuses, grew by 3.7% in the three months to August compared with the same period in 2025, the Office for National Statistics said, extending a gradual pickup since touching a low of 3.4% earlier this year. A Reuters poll of economists had pointed to a weaker increase of 3.6%. The figure for the three months to July was revised up slightly to show a rise of 3.6%. A preliminary measure of payrolled employees from Britain's tax office rose by 13,000 in the month of September. The change for August was revised to show a rise of 1,000 compared with a provisional estimate of a decline of 26,000. The unemployment rate - which is derived from a survey that the ONS is overhauling - dropped to 4.7% in the three months to August, its lowest since mid-2025.

stories.title: European bonus point system met with provincial optimism
stories.summary: Leinster assistant coach Tyler Bleyendaal and centre Garry Ringrose have said that they are fans of the new try bonus point rule that was launched in the Investec Champions Cup, and EPCR Challenge Cup over the weekend. In a system based on France's Top 14 and Super Rugby in the southern hemisphere, a team can only earn a try bonus point if they outscore their opponent by three tries. Leinster were one of only six teams to register the added table point over the weekend, despite 16 of the 24 sides scoring four or more. For Bleyendaal, who is more than familiar with the model from his coaching days with the Hurricanes, there is merit in keeping the new format. "It definitely adds another dimension and I think it's a positive one as well", the attack coach said. "Teams can get four tries and then they might start playing differently just to get over the line, but you can't let another team come back into it. Your substitutions, they've got to come on and have a real impact on the game and I think it's going to be positive for the spectator.
